content: Each year, approximately 4 million Americans who were previously unaffected contract trichomoniasis. The causative agent of trichomoniasis is Trichomonas vaginalis, an anaerobic, flagellated protozoan parasite. This organism was first identified in 1836 by Dr. Alfred François Donné, a French physician. The parasite is transmitted sexually through contact with an infected partner. Women can acquire the infection from either infected men or women, whereas men typically contract it only from infected women. Trichomoniasis primarily affects the genitourinary tract. In men, the urethra is the most common site of infection, while in women, the vagina is the primary site. It is essential to distinguish trichomoniasis from other causes of vaginitis, such as bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and atrophic vaginitis. In 2008, the incidence of trichomoniasis in the United States was estimated at 358 cases per 100,000 individuals. Women are more frequently affected than men. Risk factors for developing trichomoniasis include having multiple sexual partners, engaging in unprotected sexual activity, intravenous drug use, and coexisting sexually transmitted infections. African American individuals are disproportionately affected, with prevalence rates in women ranging from 13% to 51%, while Caucasian individuals are less commonly affected. If left untreated, trichomoniasis in women can lead to infections of the adnexa, endometrium, and Skene and Bartholin glands. In men, untreated trichomoniasis may result in epididymitis, prostatitis, and reduced sperm motility. Complications of trichomoniasis include pelvic inflammatory disease, an increased risk of HIV acquisition, a higher likelihood of cervical and prostate cancers, and pregnancy-related complications such as low birth weight, preterm delivery, and premature rupture of membranes. However, with appropriate treatment, the prognosis for trichomoniasis is generally excellent. The majority of individuals with trichomoniasis are asymptomatic—85% of women and 77% of men. Among asymptomatic women, one-third develop symptoms within six months. Common symptoms in women include diffuse, malodorous, yellow-green or gray vaginal discharge; painful urination (dysuria); vulvar irritation and itching; abdominal pain; and discomfort during sexual intercourse. In men, symptoms may include clear or mucopurulent urethral discharge, painful urination, and itching or a burning sensation after sexual intercourse. Physical examination findings in women with trichomoniasis may reveal a strawberry cervix and a foul-smelling, frothy, mucopurulent green or gray vaginal discharge. In men, there may be scant mucopurulent urethral discharge. Laboratory tests used to diagnose trichomoniasis include saline microscopy, culture, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). The primary treatment for trichomoniasis is antimicrobial therapy, typically with a single oral dose of metronidazole. Symptoms in infected men may resolve spontaneously within a few weeks without treatment, but untreated men can continue to infect or reinfect female partners. Therefore, it is crucial to treat both partners simultaneously to eradicate the parasite. Individuals undergoing treatment should abstain from sexual activity until both they and their partners have completed treatment and are symptom-free. Metronidazole is safe for use during pregnancy. Importantly, having trichomoniasis once does not confer immunity, and reinfection is possible after successful treatment. Primary prevention strategies include abstinence from sexual contact and consistent, correct use of latex male condoms, which can reduce the risk of transmission. Any genital symptoms, such as discharge, burning during urination, or unusual sores or rashes, should prompt individuals to cease sexual activity and seek immediate medical evaluation.
